passage:
"You didn't say a word all the way home," Irfan said on the bus.
"He called me a waste of a jersey. In front of the whole team."
"Again?"
"Tuesday is the worst. My stomach hurts before I even get to the ground."
"Abhinav, extra laps, hard drills, being told your pass was lazy, that's tough training. Being shouted at and shamed until you dread going, that's different."
"But we win because of him."
"Winning doesn't need the shouting."
"And last week he grabbed my arm really hard. It felt wrong."
"Then you tell your mother tonight, and the sports teacher. I'll come with you."
Abhinav looked out at the road and nodded.

qa.q: What did the coach call Abhinav in front of the team?
What was Abhinav feeling on Tuesdays before practice, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Dread. His stomach hurt before he even reached the ground.

qa.q: What difference does Irfan draw between tough training and something worse?
qa.a: Extra laps, hard drills and honest feedback are tough training. Shouting and shaming until someone dreads going, or grabbing that feels wrong, is not okay and should be told to a parent or school official.

qa.q: How does Irfan see Abhinav's situation compared with his own view of the coach's results?
qa.a: He accepts that the team wins but insists winning does not need shouting. He offers to go along, so he treats it as serious and wants Abhinav not to face it alone.

grounding: A coach shames players to win; a friend helps distinguish tough training from abuse and urges telling adults.

passage:
At the school football ground, Urmila ma'am's whistle could be heard two streets away. Hard drills, early practice, laps in the rain: Jomon didn't mind that. That was training.
But lately it was different. When a boy missed a pass, she made him stand in the centre circle while she told everyone he was "useless, a disgrace to the team." Last week she'd done it to Jomon. The others had been told to clap.
He started dreading Tuesdays. His stomach hurt before every session.
On Thursday, after she made a Class 8 boy cry in front of everyone, Jomon went straight to the sports office. He told the head of sports, Mr Fernandes, exactly what had happened, with the dates.
Mr Fernandes listened and said, "Tough training is one thing. Humiliating players is not. Thank you for telling me." He called Jomon's parents that afternoon and spoke to Urmila ma'am before the next session.

qa.q: Where did Urmila ma'am make players stand?
How did Jomon feel about football practice lately?
qa.a: He felt dread, his stomach hurting before every session, after being humiliated in front of the team.

qa.q: What did Jomon do, and why was it wise?
qa.a: He separated tough training from humiliation and reported it with dates to Mr Fernandes, who acted the same day.

qa.q: How does Mr Fernandes see Urmila ma'am's behaviour?
qa.a: He sees it as humiliation, not tough training, and takes it seriously by calling Jomon's parents and speaking to her.

grounding: A teen who dreads a coach who shames players distinguishes tough training from abuse and reports it to a school official.

passage:
Dear Didi,
You asked why I stopped talking about hockey. I'll tell you properly.
Coach Manoj used to be tough, which was fine. Running, drills, no excuses. But this term he started shaming us. If someone missed a shot, he'd call them "a girl" or "a waste of food" in front of everyone. Once he grabbed my collar and shouted in my face. I started feeling sick every morning before practice.
At first I thought maybe that's just how coaching is. Then I remembered you saying that tough is fine, but humiliation isn't.
On Monday I told Mummy and Papa everything. Papa went with me to the principal on Tuesday morning. The principal said, "Thank you for coming. This is not acceptable," and moved our practice to the PE teacher while they look into it.
I miss the game. But I feel lighter now. Call me Sunday?
Your brother,
Mridul

qa.q: What did Coach Manoj call players who missed a shot?
How did Mridul feel before practice this term?
qa.a: He felt sick with dread every morning because of the coach's shaming and shouting.
Remembering that tough is fine but humiliation isn't, telling his parents, and going to the principal, who acted right away.

qa.q: How does the principal respond to Mridul and Papa?
qa.a: The principal takes it seriously, calls the behaviour unacceptable and moves practice to the PE teacher while looking into it.

grounding: A teen who dreads a coach who shames players sees it is abuse, not tough training, and tells his parents and the principal.
